newsitem.title: USA: AT&T's Walter resigns; had been heir-apparent.
newsitem.headline: AT&T's Walter resigns; had been heir-apparent.

text.p: AT&T Corp. said on Wednesday that its president, John Walter, resigned nearly nine months after he was chosen as the heir-apparent to Chief Executive Officer Robert Allen.

The company said its board voted not to promote Walter to chief executive officer, succeeding Allen. At the time of his appointment last October, some industry officials wondered whether Walter, former chairman of printer R.R. Donnelley & Sons, would be able to lead AT&T effectively in the highly competitive telecommunications market.

Walter, 50, appointed in October, joined AT&T last November and was expected to succeed Allen as CEO in January 1998. The resignation came after the board decided it was not ready to name him CEO on the schedule originally discussed, the nation's largest long-distance company said.

The resignation followed months of speculation that Walter might be passed over as Allen's successor if AT&T's reported merger talks with SBC Communications Inc. led to a merger. SBC Chairman Ed Whiteacre was said to be in line to replace Allen as head of the combined company.

The AT&T board also said a special committee would conduct a search for a CEO and recommend a successor. It also named John Zeglis, 50, only recently named vice chairman, to lead AT&T operations, with operating heads reporting to Zeglis.
A company director said Zeglis was likely to be one of 10 candidates for the CEO position.

The company's law, government affairs, human resources and public relations departments, which now report to Zeglis, will report directly to Allen. The recent elevation of Zeglis to vice chairman had stoked further speculation that Walter's career at AT&T was in danger.

Zeglis had previously served as AT&T's chief corporate counsel and head of government regulatory affairs among other duties. He has held a variety of responsibilities in the past year of turmoil among the senior ranks of management at AT&T.
AT&T's stock jumped more than $1 to $36.31 following news of Walter's resignation.
Under the terms of his employment contract with AT&T, Walter, who also resigned as a director of the company, will receive about $3.8 million in separation payments.
That is in addition to the compensation package of about $22 million AT&T provided him to replace salary, pension and bonuses he forfeited when he left Donnelley.

"John Walter is an energetic leader who made important contributions to AT&T in a relatively short period," said Walter Elisha, an AT&T director and chairman and chief executive of Springs Industries Inc.

"But the Board has decided it will not elect him CEO by next January, as originally foreseen. Therefore, John has decided to leave the company, exercising rights under his employment contract, and we wish him well," Elisha said.
In AT&T's statement, Walter said his immediate plans were uncertain.
"I believe I am perfectly qualified to be CEO of AT&T right now," he said. "I have worked tirelessly on behalf of the shareholders of AT&T."
